title: Block 1 Knowledge Check — Professional Judgement, Live Conduct and Calibration

questions.question: Which statement best describes the purpose of recurrent examiner professional development?

answers.text: Repeat the initial Examiner Course every two years.
Maintain currency, reflection, evidence discipline and examiner calibration.
Ensure every examiner uses an identical assessment technique.
Replace the examiner’s responsibility to remain current with regulatory material.

questions.feedback: Correct response: B. Recurrent development assumes foundational knowledge is already established. Its purpose is to maintain current, reflective and standardised professional practice.

questions.question: An experienced examiner’s professional intuition:

answers.text: Can replace recorded evidence when the examiner has extensive operational experience.
Should be excluded because intuition cannot contribute to a fair assessment.
Should take priority whenever the published standard leaves room for judgement.
Can identify patterns, but conclusions must still be supported by evidence and the applicable standard.

questions.feedback: Correct response: D. Experience can sharpen recognition, but assessment conclusions must remain anchored to observable evidence and the applicable standard.

questions.question: You are assessing a familiar, well-regarded candidate while the operator is short of qualified personnel. Which information should carry the greatest weight?

answers.text: The observable evidence from today’s assessment.
The operator’s confidence in the candidate.
The candidate’s previous strong performance.
The operational consequences of an unsuccessful outcome.

questions.feedback: Preferred response: A. Previous performance and operational context may influence the examiner, but they do not replace evidence from the current assessment.

questions.question: A candidate enters one digit of a radio frequency incorrectly, then independently identifies and corrects it after no response. What is the best examiner response?

answers.text: Treat the incorrect entry as conclusive evidence that the communications standard was not met.
Treat the event as resolved because the candidate restored communication without assistance.
Continue and assess the error, recognition and recovery in context with the wider evidence.
Identify the incorrect digit, then assess only the quality of the candidate’s correction.

questions.feedback: Preferred response: C. The error is observable evidence, but its significance depends on context, recognition, independence, recovery, recurrence and the applicable standard. Recovery adds evidence; it does not erase the original error.

questions.question: A highly experienced candidate has strong technical skill, the operator is short of personnel, and a significant lapse in judgement appears near the end of the assessment. Which question should the examiner answer first?

answers.text: How seriously would the operator be affected by an unsuccessful outcome?
What exactly was observed, and which standard or competency does it relate to?
How strong was the candidate’s technical performance during the rest of the test?
Would failing the candidate be disproportionate after an otherwise strong test?

questions.feedback: Preferred response: B. The decision process must begin with observable evidence and its relationship to the standard, not operational consequence or reputation.

questions.question: The evidence is significant but isolated, and there is no further valid opportunity to gather more evidence. Which statement is most appropriate?

answers.text: An isolated event cannot determine the outcome unless the same behaviour is observed again.
Strong technical performance should outweigh an isolated judgement concern near the end.
The candidate should receive the benefit of the doubt whenever further evidence is unavailable.
A single event may be decisive when its severity and relationship to the standard justify that weight.

questions.feedback: Preferred response: D. Pattern matters, but severity matters too. Consider context, consequence, independence, recovery and the precise requirements of the standard.

questions.question: Which debrief statement is more defensible?

answers.text: During the arrival you missed conflicting traffic twice and did not re-establish the scan until after the traffic alert.
The situational-awareness standard was not achieved because the overall arrival did not meet expectations.
Your traffic scan was weaker than would normally be expected from a candidate at this level.
The arrival was concerning, and further situational-awareness training should be completed.

questions.feedback: Preferred response: A. It describes observable behaviour and provides a clearer evidence trail for the assessment judgement.

questions.question: In the mixed-evidence workshop, an administrative prerequisite appears incomplete although the operator says the underlying training was completed. What should drive the commencement decision?

answers.text: The candidate’s likely competence, supported by past performance and operator assurance.
Whether every required precondition for a valid assessment has been verified.
The operational need, provided the missing record is corrected after the assessment.
The examiner’s previous knowledge, with the prerequisite noted for later confirmation.

questions.feedback: Preferred response: B. Competence and assessment validity are related but separate. Confirm that the assessment can legitimately commence within current requirements and authority.

questions.question: During a later high-workload phase, the candidate misses a radio call, omits one checklist item and allows navigation accuracy to deteriorate. Each event is recoverable. What should the examiner do?

answers.text: Treat the cluster as a failed standard because three errors have occurred under workload.
Treat each event as resolved because recovery occurred before a lasting consequence.
Prompt the candidate to manage workload, then assess the response to that direction.
Continue gathering evidence to decide whether the events form a meaningful performance pattern.

questions.feedback: Preferred response: D. Separate isolated error from emerging pattern. Prompting may contaminate evidence unless needed for safety.

questions.question: During a later phase, the candidate enters a frequency incorrectly, initially repeats the call, then independently identifies and corrects the entry. Which statement is most accurate?

answers.text: Assess the error, recognition and recovery together, then decide whether the event is isolated or part of a pattern.
Treat the incorrect frequency as decisive because communication accuracy is required throughout.
Treat the event as resolved because communication was restored without examiner assistance.
Give the correct frequency after the first unanswered call, then assess the correction.

questions.feedback: Preferred response: A. The incorrect entry, recognition and independent recovery are all relevant evidence. Avoid an automatic outcome based on one procedural error.

questions.question: After a frequency error, the candidate demonstrates stronger cross-checking and performs the remaining items well. How should the recovery be treated?

answers.text: It replaces the earlier error because the candidate changed the checking behaviour.
It should be excluded because only performance at the time of the error is relevant.
It is useful evidence that must be weighed with the original event rather than replacing it.
It proves competence because the correction required no examiner assistance.

questions.feedback: Preferred response: C. Recovery can demonstrate recognition, checking discipline and effective correction, but it does not remove the original evidence.

questions.question: When operational pressure exists, which factor should determine the assessment standard applied?

answers.text: Candidate experience and previous results when operational consequences are significant.
Published requirements and the evidence gathered during the current assessment.
Operator needs and the availability of another candidate or suitable aircraft.
Examiner familiarity with how the candidate normally performs under pressure.

questions.feedback: Correct response: B. Operational pressure may be real, but it does not alter the applicable standard or the evidence required.

questions.question: What is the best description of examiner drift in this programme?

answers.text: Any change an examiner makes to a preferred assessment technique over time.
Any difference of opinion between two examiners considering the same event.
A formal CAA action taken after an examiner applies a standard incorrectly.
Gradual movement away from shared interpretation or application of the required standard.

questions.feedback: Correct response: D. Professional practice should evolve. Drift refers to movement away from shared standards or their consistent application.

questions.question: A candidate enters an incorrect frequency, recognises it independently and corrects it. What should the examiner do?

answers.text: Consider the error and recovery in context with the wider evidence and applicable standard.
Ignore the original error because the candidate recovered without examiner assistance.
Treat the incorrect entry as an automatic failure against the communications standard.
Repeat the exercise to obtain another result before assigning any assessment weight.

questions.feedback: Correct response: A. The original error and the independent recovery are both relevant evidence and must be considered with the wider assessment pattern and standard.

questions.question: How should strong recovery after an error be treated?

answers.text: It cancels the original error when the correction is prompt and independent.
It should be excluded because the original error remains part of the record.
It is additional evidence that must be weighed with the original event.
It changes an unsuccessful outcome when the remainder of the test is strong.

questions.feedback: Correct response: C. Recovery may demonstrate recognition and resilience, but it does not erase the original evidence.

questions.question: Which note is most defensible?

answers.text: Candidate appeared uncertain and made several poor decisions during the approach.
Situational awareness was below the level expected for an experienced candidate.
Continued approach after agreed stabilisation criteria were not met.
Candidate seemed stressed and did not manage the flight as confidently as expected.

questions.feedback: Correct response: C. The strongest note records specific observable behaviour that can be linked to the standard.
